config.title: Min Stack

intro.title: Min Stack
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a 'Min Stack' data structure that supports standard stack operations (push, pop, top) and can also retrieve the minimum element in constant time. You will learn how to use two stacks—one for storing all values and another to track the minimum values—to efficiently maintain the minimum. The main technologies involved are JavaScript arrays, which act as stacks, and basic conditional logic. This exercise will help you understand how to design data structures that optimize for specific operations while keeping your code clean and efficient.
intro.usecase: The Min Stack pattern is essential in real-time systems where you need to track minimum values efficiently, such as stock trading dashboards that display the lowest price of the day while processing continuous price updates. It's also used in e-commerce carts to show the cheapest item in the cart as users add or remove products, and in gaming leaderboards to maintain the lowest score among active players. This data structure ensures O(1) time complexity for retrieving minimum values, making it ideal for performance-critical UI components like financial charts, inventory management systems, and real-time analytics panels.

objectives: Construct a MinStack class with a constructor that initializes two arrays for primary storage and minimum tracking.
Implement a push method that adds a value to the stack while updating the current minimum.
Implement a pop method that removes the top element from the stack and updates the minimum tracking accordingly.
Apply a top method to retrieve the last element added to the stack without removing it.
Manipulate the getMin method to return the current minimum element in constant time.
Integrate the MinStack methods to handle edge cases such as an empty stack.

content.body: Imagine you're stacking plates in a cafeteria. You can only take the top plate off the pile. Now, what if you also needed to instantly know which plate is the smallest in the entire stack? That's the Min Stack problem. We'll build a special stack that tracks its minimum element efficiently.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
• Explain why a regular stack can't track its minimum efficiently.
• Implement a Min Stack using two internal stacks.
• Determine when to push and pop from the minimum-tracking stack.
• Analyze the constant-time performance of all operations.
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Think about a regular stack of plates. You can push (add) a new plate to the top, and pop (remove) the top plate. If someone asks, 'What's the smallest plate in the stack right now?', how would you find it? You'd have to look through the entire pile, right? That's slow if the stack is large.
content.title: Try it

content.body: You just identified the core challenge: a regular stack gives you fast access to the top (last-in, first-out), but finding the minimum requires checking every element. That's O(n) time, which doesn't scale well.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When the stack has thousands of plates (or numbers), scanning through all of them every time we need the minimum becomes very inefficient. We need a way to always know the current minimum instantly, without searching.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Remember the stack mental model: Last-In, First-Out (LIFO), like a pile of plates. We can only directly access the top plate. To track the minimum, we'll use a second, parallel stack that only stores the current minimum at each point in time. When we push a new plate, we compare it to the current minimum on our helper stack. When we pop, we also pop from the helper stack, so it always reflects the minimum of what's left.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Stack: pile of plates. Queue: people in a line.

content.body: We'll maintain two stacks: one for all values (the main stack), and another (minStack) that tracks the current minimum. When pushing a new value, we push it to the main stack. We also push to minStack, but only if it's less than or equal to the current top of minStack (or if minStack is empty). When popping, we pop from both stacks. The top of minStack will always be the minimum of the main stack.
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. Initialize two empty arrays: `stack` and `minStack`.
2. On `push(val)`: push `val` to `stack`. If `minStack` is empty or `val` ≤ top of `minStack`, push `val` to `minStack`.
3. On `pop()`: pop from `stack`. If the popped value equals the top of `minStack`, also pop from `minStack`.
4. `getMin()`: return the top of `minStack`.
5. `top()`: return the top of `stack`.
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Set up the class
steps.instruction: Create a MinStack class with a constructor. Initialize two empty arrays: one for the main stack and one to track minimums.
steps.expectedOutcome: A class definition with two empty array properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've set up the foundation for our two-stack solution.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Remember to create both stack arrays.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's start fresh. The constructor should initialize two empty arrays.

steps.title: Implement push
steps.instruction: Add a push method that takes a value. Push it to the main stack. Then, if the minStack is empty OR the value is less than or equal to the current minimum (top of minStack), also push it to minStack.
steps.expectedOutcome: A push method that updates both stacks conditionally.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You're correctly tracking the minimum as we add values.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Remember to push to minStack only under the right conditions.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's review: always push to main stack, but only push to minStack if it's empty or val ≤ current min.

steps.title: Implement pop
steps.instruction: Add a pop method. First, pop from the main stack and store the value. If that popped value equals the current minimum (top of minStack), also pop from minStack. You don't need to return anything.
steps.hint: Use `const popped = this.stack.pop()`. Then check if `popped === this.minStack[this.minStack.length-1]`.
steps.expectedOutcome: A pop method that removes elements from both stacks when needed.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! You're maintaining the invariant that minStack's top always matches the current minimum.
steps.feedbackPartial: Close. Remember to compare the popped value with the top of minStack.
steps.feedbackWrong: Think it through: pop from main stack, then if that value equals the top of minStack, pop from minStack too.

steps.title: Implement top
steps.instruction: Add a top method that returns the top element of the main stack without removing it.
steps.expectedOutcome: A top method that returns the last element of the main stack array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Well done! This gives us standard stack peek functionality.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. Remember to return the element, not remove it.
steps.feedbackWrong: The top method should return the last element of `this.stack`.

steps.title: Implement getMin
steps.instruction: Add a getMin method that returns the current minimum element (the top of minStack).
steps.expectedOutcome: A getMin method that returns the top of the minStack.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! Now we can retrieve the minimum in constant time.
steps.feedbackPartial: Close. The minimum is stored at the top of the minStack.
steps.feedbackWrong: getMin should return the last element of `this.minStack`.

steps.title: Test the implementation
steps.instruction: Create an instance of MinStack and test the operations. Push values 5, 3, 4, then call getMin, pop, and getMin again. Observe how the minimum changes.
steps.hint: Instantiate with `const obj = new MinStack()`, then call the methods in order.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! Your MinStack correctly tracks the minimum through pushes and pops.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check the order of operations. After pushing 5,3,4, the minimum is 3.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's trace: push 5 (min=5), push 3 (min=3), push 4 (min stays 3), pop 4 (min still 3), pop 3 (min goes back to 5).

content.body: Congratulations! You've implemented a Min Stack that supports push, pop, top, and getMin all in O(1) time. The key insight was using a second stack to track the minimum at each point. Remember: stacks are LIFO (last-in, first-out), and this two-stack approach is a classic pattern for augmenting a stack with extra information efficiently.
